{{Short description|Type of Diophantine equation in number theory}}
In [[number theory]], the '''Ramanujan–Nagell equation''' is an [[equation (mathematics)| 
equation]] between a [[square number]] and a number that is seven less than a [[power of two]]. It is an example of an [[exponential Diophantine equation]], an equation to be solved in integers where one of the variables appears as an [[Exponentiation|exponent]].

The equation is named after [[Srinivasa Ramanujan]], who conjectured that it has only five [[integer]] solutions, and after [[Trygve Nagell]], who proved the conjecture. It implies non-existence of [[perfect code|perfect binary codes]] with the minimum [[Hamming distance]] 5 or 6.

==Equation and solution==
The equation is
:<math>2^n-7=x^2 \,</math>
and solutions in [[Natural number|natural numbers]] ''n'' and ''x'' exist just when ''n'' = 3, 4, 5, 7 and 15 {{OEIS|A060728}}.

This was conjectured in 1913 by Indian [[mathematician]] [[Srinivasa Ramanujan]], proposed independently in 1943 by the Norwegian mathematician [[Wilhelm Ljunggren]], and proved in 1948 by the Norwegian mathematician [[Trygve Nagell]]. The values of ''n'' correspond to the values of ''x'' as:-

:''x'' = 1, 3, 5, 11 and 181 {{OEIS|A038198}}.{{Sfn|Saradha|Srinivasan|2008|p=208}}

== Triangular Mersenne numbers ==
The problem of finding all numbers of the form 2<sup>''b''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 ([[Mersenne number]]s) which are [[triangular number|triangular]] is equivalent:

:<math>
\begin{align}
& \ 2^b-1 = \frac{y(y+1)}{2} \\[2pt]
\Longleftrightarrow & \ 8(2^b-1) = 4y(y+1) \\
\Longleftrightarrow & \ 2^{b+3}-8 = 4y^2+4y \\
\Longleftrightarrow & \ 2^{b+3}-7 = 4y^2+4y+1 \\
\Longleftrightarrow & \ 2^{b+3}-7 = (2y+1)^2
\end{align}
</math>

The values of ''b'' are just those of ''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;3, and the corresponding triangular Mersenne numbers (also known as '''Ramanujan–Nagell numbers''') are:

:<math>\frac{y(y+1)}{2} = \frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{8}</math>

for ''x'' = 1, 3, 5, 11 and 181, giving 0, 1, 3, 15, 4095 and no more {{OEIS|A076046}}.

==Equations of Ramanujan–Nagell type==
An equation of the form

:<math> x^2 + D = A B^n </math>

for fixed ''D'', ''A'', ''B'' and variable ''x'', ''n'' is said to be of ''Ramanujan–Nagell type''.  The result of [[Carl Ludwig Siegel|Siegel]]{{Sfn|Siegel|1929}} implies that the number of solutions in each case is finite.{{Sfn|Saradha|Srinivasan|2008|p=207}} By representing <math>n = 3m + r</math> with <math>r\in\{0,1,2\}</math> and <math>B^n = B^r y^3</math> with <math>y=B^m</math>, the equation of Ramanujan–Nagell type is reduced to three [[Mordell curve]]s (indexed by <math>r</math>), each of which has a finite number of integer solutions:
: <math>r=0:\qquad (Ax)^2 = (Ay)^3 - A^2D</math>,
: <math>r=1:\qquad (ABx)^2 = (ABy)^3 - A^2B^2D</math>,
: <math>r=2:\qquad (AB^2x)^2 = (AB^2y)^3 - A^2B^4D</math>.

The equation with <math>A=1,\ B=2,\ D>0</math> has at most two solutions, except in the case <math>D=7</math> corresponding to the Ramanujan–Nagell equation. This does not hold for <math>D<0</math>, such as <math>D=-17</math>, where <math> x^2 - 17 = 2^n </math> has the four solutions <math>(x,n) = (5,3),(7,5),(9,6),(23,9)</math>. In general, if <math>D=-(4^k-3\cdot2^{k+1}+1)</math> for an integer <math>k\geqslant3</math> there are at least the four solutions
: <math>(x,n) = \begin{cases}(2^k-3,3)\\(2^k-1,k+2)\\(2^k+1,k+3)\\(3\cdot2^k-1,2k+3)\end{cases}</math>
and these are the only four if <math>D>-10^{12}</math>.{{Sfn|Beukers|1981|p=401-403}} There are infinitely many values of ''D'' for which there are exactly two solutions, including <math>D = 2^m - 1</math>.{{Sfn|Saradha|Srinivasan|2008|p=208}}

==Equations of Lebesgue–Nagell type==
An equation of the form

:<math> x^2 + D = A y^n </math>

for fixed ''D'', ''A'' and variable ''x'', ''y'', ''n'', where ''n'' > 2, is said to be of ''Lebesgue–Nagell type''.  This is named after [[Victor-Amédée Lebesgue]], who proved that the equation

:<math> x^2 + 1 = y^n </math>

has no nontrivial solutions.{{Sfn|Lebesgue|1850}}

Results of Shorey and [[Robert Tijdeman|Tijdeman]]{{Sfn|Shorey|Tijdeman|1986}} imply that the number of solutions in each case is finite.{{Sfn|Saradha|Srinivasan|2008|p=211}} Bugeaud, Mignotte and Siksek{{Sfn|Bugeaud|Mignotte|Siksek|2006}} solved equations of this type with ''A'' = 1 and 1 &le; ''D'' &le; 100. In particular, the following generalization of the Ramanujan–Nagell equation:
:<math>y^n=x^2+7 \,</math>
has positive integer solutions only when ''x'' = 1, 3, 5, 11, or 181.
